title: What you should own after a studio engagement
metaTitle: Website code ownership after a build
excerpt: Website code ownership means the repository, the domain, the analytics, and the content logins sit with you. A studio that keeps those is a dependency.
alt: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table. The shared table fits a piece about who actually holds the accounts when the work is done.
caption: After the build, the accounts should be in your name. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a client own after a studio builds a site?
faqs.answer: The repository, the domain, the hosting account, the analytics property, and the logins for the CMS or any other place content is edited. You should be able to change a password and still have the site. If a single vendor login is the only way to reach the work, you do not own it yet.

faqs.question: Is it enough to have a copy of the files?
faqs.answer: A zip of the files is a start and not ownership. You need the repository with its history, the right to deploy, and the accounts that the domain points at. A copy you cannot ship is a souvenir. The live site would still depend on someone else's keys.

faqs.question: What can the studio keep?
faqs.answer: Its own process, its internal notes, and any tools it licenses for itself. It should not keep the only admin role on your domain, your repository, or your analytics. Access for support can be granted and revoked. Ownership stays with the company that the site represents.

markdown:
Website code ownership is a list you can check on the day a project ends. You own the repository. You own the domain. You own the analytics. You own the content logins. A studio that keeps those is a dependency, not a partner, however pleasant the working relationship was. The site represents your company. The keys should too.

This is not a hostile stance. A good studio will put the accounts in your name from the start, and accept access that you can remove. The test is what happens if you never speak again. The site should keep running, and someone you hire next should be able to change it.

## The repository

The code lives in a repository under an account your company controls. GitHub, or whatever host you both agreed, in your organization. The studio's users are collaborators. They are not the owner. History stays. A zip file emailed at the end is not a repository. It has no history, no connection to the host, and no obvious way to deploy.

The README says how to run the project and how a change gets to the public site. Secrets are not hard-coded. They live in the host's environment, and you can see the list of names even when the values are hidden. A next developer should reach a staging URL by following the document, without a private tour.

Hanabi builds in Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, and hands that stack over in the client's repository. The particular tools matter less than the pattern. Ordinary, readable code in an account you control. A bespoke platform that only the original authors can boot is a rented site with extra steps.

## The domain and the host

The domain registrar account is yours. The DNS is somewhere you can log in. The host that serves the site, such as Vercel, is in your team, with billing visible to you. If the studio's credit card is the only thing keeping the site online, you will discover the arrangement during an emergency.

Write down where DNS is managed. It is often not the same login as the registrar, and it is not the same login as the host. Three doors, three owners, and you should be all three, or your company should. A studio can hold a delegate role for the launch week. Delegate is not owner.

Ask for the rollback before you need it. What is the previous deployment, and who can promote it? If the answer is a person at the studio and a login you have never seen, you do not yet own production. Fix that while the project is still friendly.

## Analytics and the other windows

Own the analytics property. The site should send data to a property inside your account. A studio can be a viewer. If the only reports live in their account, your history leaves when they do, and you cannot prove what the site did.

Own the form destination, the email inboxes the site sends to, and the error log if there is one. Own the CMS admin. Own the store admin if you sell anything. Make a list of every login the site depends on, and mark whose email is the owner. Personal inboxes of contractors are a common and bad answer. Use a company address that more than one person can recover.

Google's page on [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) is a small example of why the CMS login matters after the contract. Titles should describe each page, and an inaccurate or outdated title is something you will need to change. If you cannot get into the tool that sets the title, you cannot keep the public description of your own pages honest. Ownership is what makes ordinary maintenance possible. It is not a legal flourish.

## What good access looks like during the work

You do not have to do the building. You do have to be the owner while it is being built. Create the accounts yourself, or create them on a call and change the password. Invite the studio in. Remove them when the intensive work ends, or leave them as guests if you still want help. The order is the point. Guests can leave. Owners should not be surprised.

Billing belongs with you even when the studio is doing the deploys. A platform bill sent only to a vendor is how a site becomes leverage in a dispute, or simply expires because a card on their side expired. You want the invoice. You want the ability to add a second admin who is not the founder, so a vacation is not an outage.

Write the list into the handoff note. Repository, host, registrar, DNS, analytics, CMS, email, any third-party script that has its own login. Next to each, the owner email and where recovery codes sit. A portal can hold that note beside the brand files. Hanabi's portal is for assets, docs, and updates, which is a reasonable shelf for this list. The shelf is not a substitute for the accounts being yours.

## The conversation to have before kickoff

Ask, in the first calls, where the repository will live and whose name will be on the domain. A studio that hesitates is telling you the default is their account. You can still hire them. Change the default before the first line of code. Migrating a live site out of someone else's organization is slower and ruder than starting in the right place.

Ask what they will need to keep if you part ways. The honest answer is nothing that the site needs in order to run. Their portfolio may show the work. The work itself, the code and the content and the name on the internet, stays with you.

Handoff is the moment this list becomes real, and it includes more than keys. [The handoff that makes a redesign usable after the studio leaves](/blog/redesign-handoff) is the next piece, about the repository, the content map, and a place the brand files live.

If you want those accounts agreed before a project starts, [book an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the question of ownership into the first conversation, not the last invoice.
